div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING. (By Redcap.)

PATENT FOODS. So many ard so numerous ate the different brands of patent poultry foods, that one is almost bewildered in making a selection of the best. There is really BO cause for lewildern.ent, in fact, there in no need to purchase patent food muffs at all, providing that yon have a good knowledge of mixing different meals. I hare been asked no many times which is the best food to buy, that I think a useful purpose will le served if I detail the question. Before Ido al, however, let ace ray that there are some patent foods which are absolutely reliable. At the same time there in no need to pay high prices for such foods when you can economically mix your own, and at the same time serve the purpone. I shall deal only with two mixings, one for voting and hummer feeding, the other for a winter diet, huh however to compose of suitable meals for a morning mash. We shall deal first with

SI.,)111E0 CI fliO. It goes witlibut saying that eurnmer feeding while being wholetione should not be overbea,ing. You will find the following a mist useful and valuable recipe .—Take two harts best biscuit meal, two parts best middlings and one part pea meal. Mix the whole well together aid you have as fine a poultry food as it is possible to get. I base ti.e.l the above with the very best results : and no one can induce me to depart from it for any patent food on the market.

ISTEII !TY 'I he above recipe only requires one alteration, that is, substitute Maize meal for the pea nieal. Of necessity the fools need more body heat in winter, thou the maize ineal fulfils the requirement. The benefit of mixing your own food-stuff lies in the fact. that you know what it contains atticles of diet which are mixed and patented, often contain unwhole- some ingredients. 'therefore by following these simple yet important instructions you profit thereby and not only will you profit in the actual egg yield but also by a reduction of expenditure. Sit ,( Et, Purchasing mixed fowl corn is another fallacy too oft. adopted. Take and closely examine a satnple of mixed corn and you will find a lot of needless and unwholesome additions therein. 'the very fact of its general use suggests to purveyors, a chance of getting rid cd light grain etc. As I write 1 have before me a sample of mixed fowl corn and I can irately say that quite 20 per cat of the grain is practically use- less. Generally speaking, fowls are greedy creatures and as you throw down the corn they " gobble" it up. But what's the use of them going to roost with a crop full of unwholesome grain:? The consequence is, that they are hungry lief. re morning ; And instead of them digesting sound grain and turning it into flesh and ti,sue, they simply pass it through the system as so much o este. As with the meals so with the corn. If you want a mixed corn Ifix it yourse'f. When doing et, see that the samples you boy are sound and of good quality. It is not advisable to give water to very young chicken.; for at least four or five days they need no moisture other than what they get from the soft (rod, and even then thev should only partake of water at their own free will. I have seen many young people take a young chick only a few hours old and dip its head into water. Do sou wonder if disaster follows ? The shock is certainly too great for the little ayatem and only a cinches of very among constitution would survive. Warmth is the great easential to young life and the realization of this factor aticuld he sufficient proof, l'ruler natural conditions c.n you imagine a ben wondering ill to the nearest brook with, batch of young chicks to have their fill of water ? Certainly not. The only di ink they get (until they are old enough to wander fail in the moisture which is absorbed in the natural foods they get. Observe as much as possible all the natural conditions, and do likewire.

div.head: INTERNATIONAL ORDER OF GOOD TEMPLARS
div.p: INTERNATIONAL ORDER OF GOOD TEMPLARS

The monthly meeting of the South-West Lancashire Convention was held last Saturday in the Spiritualist Hall, Wargreve-road, Earlestown. The Lodge was duly opened by Bro. Punshon, Convention Chief Templar, at 3.15. The Ctovention Secretary gay.. a report of the last convention quarter. Bro. Clarke proposed tint a letter of sympathy and condolence he sent to the relatives of the late Bro. Warburton. Bro. Watson seconded and the motion was carried. The lint of the lodges repre- sented there were as follows —The Ideal Lodge and the Temperance Misaio• Lodge, Warrington ; the Bonehill Branch Lodge, Latchford, Mid-Cheshire Dis- trict ; Stu of Widnes and the Consolation Lodge, Widnes ; Rue Welcome Lodge and the Gordon Sea- men's Lodge, Liverpool ; N,l Desperandum Lodge, Wigan ; Hope of Earlestown Lodge and the l'ioneer Lodge, St. Ifelens.—The most distinguished visitors there were Bro. It. D. Pettlson, District Chief Templar, and Bro. A. Francis, District Secretsry.—Bro. Pettison was :faked to take the chair, and be willingly accepted it—lt was proposed by Bro. Watson that the next Con. vent.° meeting be held at the Star of Widnes Lodge Bro. Clarke seconded it end the motion was carried. The Chairman was next asked to gives speech and he spoke of the great success of the convention at Darling- ton and alec the success of the lodges in the. South West Lanushire district. The lodge was afterwards closed at 5.90 by Bro. jettison, The tnembera and visitors present were flft3-seven. The audience nest sat down to tea which had been kindly prepared by the membere of the Earlestown lodge and it proved • great success. It had been arranged that ogen-nir meetings be held in some of the etreets around .bout the lodge, but owing to the conditions of the weather the meeting• were abandoned. The meeting lath. evening was npened by the Chairman, tile Rev. A. M. Mitchell, of Burton. wood, at 7.50. The meeting was opened by singing • brim, the Chairman afterwards delivering • splendid speech eboist the drink traffic and other different ques- tions. It was • splendid meeting, and the liall was full of people. A memorial service was held in the sante hall on Tueeday night in memory of the late Bro. Warburton, who had just lately panned away. Bro. Woods, Chief Templar, opened the meeting ami Bros. Clarke,Newman :and Woods related to the life of the late Bro. Warburton, who it was stated Ind been a life-long teetotaller and had also been in the Order for 39 tear,.

Cricket Notes. There was nothing particularly thrilling shout Warrington's match with St. Helena Recreation at the glass and pill town on Saturday, the result being of that delightfully indefinite order which affords little satisfaction, even to the enthusiast. It might, how. ever, have been much worse fr m the Warrington point if view, for till hat Amen fared badly in the early stages of the game and six wickets were down for 415. J. W. Pearson and W. Richardson, however, put a decidedly different complexion on the situation sod the Warringtonians were enabled to declare their innings at the respectable figure of 138 for six wickets. ISt. Ilelens were fully equal to the task of raving the game and had lost only three wickets for 91 when Imatilit les cea,ed.

Although the wicket wae on the fast ride, the I Warrington batsmen were a long t rne in getting into form and rune came slowly. Pestell, the professional, was particularly unlucky, f• r after placing one to the leg.boundary he was caught at mid-on. J. Callon and S. Partridge gave very patient but none the less useful displays, their respective scores being 26 and 15. With nix wickets down at 115 J. W. Pearson joined W. Richardson. The partnership war an eminently happy one for Warrirgton and lasted throughout the game. Both batsmen played capital forcing cricket and defied all chmgea of bowlers, Richard:on placing 39 to his credit and J. W. Pearson 33.

With on hour and a half in which to save the match, St. Helena made a promising start, and the score bad reached 45 before a wicket fell. W. div.head: UNAPPRECIATED GIFTS.
div.p: UNAPPRECIATED GIFTS.

Some of Nature's greatest gifts are not appreciated as they should be. They are too cheap to meet nab the esteem they richly deserve. Many people do not value fresh air, simply because it is not expensive. If by some means the finest Scotch beef were offered to the public at Bd. per lb., what a rush there would be to secure a share. Beef is thought by many to be the moat nutritious substance that money can buy. In olden days, before dietetics were taken up seriously by men of science, and analysts disclosed the actual amount of nutritious matter, water, fibre, etc., con- tained in the various foodstuffs, cettain modern dia- cosmic. would have been ridiculed. Even a few years ago had anyone huts recognised authority been bold enough to compare Currants with lean beef, few would have given the subject the consideration it merits. Now, however, analysts have proved their actual worth, and we know there is nothing in food value to compare with Currants. Currants are full of nutriment of the finest kind, vir„ grape sugar. They are concentrated food consisting of 90 per cent, soluble matter, and over SO per cent, pure nutriment. There is aims little tartaric acid in the composition of the Currant which gives it a delicious piquancy.

div.head: UNIVERSITY INSTRUCTION FOR WORKPEOPLE.
div.p: UNIVERSITY INSTRUCTION FOR WORKPEOPLE.
An Important Proposal.

There is n movement on foot for enabling Warring- ton to share eith many towns in Lancashire and else- I where in the advantages of a recent development in the ' education of workpeople. We refer to the suggeetion that a University Tutorial Class should be started in Warrington. It is certain that the nature of the pro- posal only needs tote understood for it to be enthusi- astically adoped and carried through. To this end few words of description are here offered. What is a University Tutorial Clean? To answer thin question adequately would require more space than can be occupied here, and moreover, would entail , language so enthuaiestic that one might be suspected of exaggeration. Let us therefore be brief and practical. The University Tutorial Class movement is an attempt I —the most serious and the most suoceeeful yet made— to provide, so Inc as circumstances allow, metruction of the highest type for those who cannot enter the walls of a univerarty. A small clam of thirty men and women enter upon the systematic study of. subject , selected by themeelves under the guidance of. tutor of the highest academic qualifications. The limited , , sirs of the class makes It possible for each student to ' have the individual attention of the tutor, who is alwas • man appointed not only for his expert I knowledge of the ',object dealt with but also for his tact and sympathy in dealing with students bandi- tcopped so heavily as workpeople necessarily are. Let it he admitted at once that entering such. class I, • terious uedertaking. The students must pledge themselvm to attend regularly and puoctmlly through three winter amnions, each comisting of 24 weekly two- hour lessons, and to write fortnightly essays on subjects set by the tutor. Many would-be students are deterred by the coropuleory emay-writing. It should be borne in mind, however, that all that is asked is that the student should do his beet to answer the questions set, that the tutor will privately, verbally, or in writing, comment on and correct the essays, that there is no comparison between the mays of different students and that the skill acquired by such constant and well- gin ded practice in putting knowledge into written form is One of the most valuable advantages gained from the clam The University provides a library of books which is usually supplemented with the aid of public and co-operative libraries. The ccst to the individual student in quite small. The fee for the whole reinter anion is never more than half • crown, and is some. times mellow as one shilling. The only charge beyond that is the price of a text-book, say three or four shillings and the cost of emery paper. Those who are prepared to fulfil the condition., reap • rich reward. They find that io joining • claire they become members of a brotherhood. The tutor is their friend and fellow•student, k now iog more of books, but ready and willing to learn from their closer and more practical knowledge of the fact. of life, lhe students, varying in experience and in point of view, have tech something to contribute to the stock of knowledge, so that a clam consists not of one teacher and thirty @chola., tut of thirty•one teacher. and thirty•one scholar., differing in almost every way, but united in their earnest desire to help one another to get at the truth.

It is the chance of sharing in such a movement that I t is suggested the workingmen and working-women of Warrington should be asked to accept. Those who wink to take advantage of it should take the opportunity [ offered for gaining full information about the propoeal. tt time same time it would be thoroughly worth while to consider the advisability of forming in Warrington • local Branch of the Woekera' Educational Association. For a Branch of the W.E.A. Weiden forming the beat agency for aucceufully eetablishing a Uni ,ty Tutorial Class, could do a great deal more for the education of the workpeople of Warrington. Even to outline the work of the W.E.A. would require another article aa long as this, but in • word it may be said that the Association is a non-pasty, unsectarisn, demo- cratic orgsnication, formed forth, purpose of arousing the interest of workpeople in education, •oiciog and satisfying their needs and wishes in regard to education, and expressing their point of view in all educational matters. There are already a hundred branches in England and Wales, and Warrington would most probably nod one as useful as any other town ken done. Anyone iotereeted aithar in the University Tutorial Class or the W.E.A. is heartily invited to apply for further information to the Secretary of the Academy- ' street Adult whool the members of which school are keenly interested. Further, it is earneetly requested that every reader will co-operate by bringing this article to the notice of all young and middle aged men and women of the town. There have been previous appeals but en exposition will be given in the Academy street Adult school to-morrow, Sunday morning, 9 30, when it is hoped • favourable decision may be arrived at.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
THE WORKIWUSE.

I cannot hr the life of me understand why the Guardians should Ito strongly object to the Rey. A. M. Mitchell's proposal to throw the Workhouse open to ratepayers on two days convenient to the authorities. Surely there is nothing very dreadful or revolutionary about the idea. It has long ago been adopted and is regularly practised in other Unions of which I have ii,,,,ig h experience,nand atlleltit.ingz. continue do tootinueaistil.ey were !rum t PALMISTRY.

I bare myself no belief whatever either in palmistry or the so-called science of phrenology; bat I know some adults, otherwiee normal, who never think of embarking upon any fresh commercial venture with- out first consulting some such "win. woman" as the Warrington Borough Bench last week punished FO severely. I have in mind one instance in particular. A former nett door neighbour of mine ("Now in heaven, poor Pilaw," as I beard a Sunday school perintendent say of a lately deceased colleague) had la lucrative situation as mill manager, but thought he could do better by going into bovines. oa , his own amount. His wife would not consent unless 1 and until he took emoted of an old fortune- teller whom she knew of. Ile therefore set off for a tramp over the bill, to the w. man's lonely dwelling In the course of the interview, she said " You are thinking of setting ap as a tranufacturer ; bat if you'll be advised by me you'll do no such thing—it would be the worst day's work you ever did, and you would certainly rue it.' He " plunged," neverthelesv, and lost heavily. After that he was not numbered In ith the unbelievers in those who profess ability to foretell coming event.. THE GIPSIES.

From what I have just written to the case of the glisten is an easy and natural transition. Once upon a time, my wife did something very like what the constables' wives did in the Warrington case the other day : she removed her wedding sing and crowd with silver the hands of one of the Boswell family in the encampment at South Shore-jail for the fun of the thing, as no doubt did many of those of our fair young townswomen who were wont to 'drop in on Madame Eloise fir a few minutes' cheap amusement. But in those days, one no more dreamed of prosecuting the Blackpool gipsies then*. diva of instituting proceedings against faehionable Wtst-end palmists or spiritualist clairvoyants, crystal-gazers, and the like in Sonthport and other popular resorts. These like the poor we have always with us ; and, in view of last week'. action at air l'olice Court, it will puzzle sine of my interested readers to know now the succesaion is to be maintained. For the Rimy— the poor gip-y -is as assuredly doomed an are the North American Indians, the Mamie@ and other aborigines. Ilere is what I read recently in the " Daily New.," when a c rrespondent drew attention to the passing of the Gipsy. "Few of the true Gipsy race remain," he wrote. "Thirty, even twenty, years ago the low tents of these wanderers, arranged con- nenienCy near a hedgerow, were frequently inet with ; to-day the nomads are only rarely seen. The ordinary van-dwellers who frequent fairs in various pat ta of the country must not be confounded with the dark-skinned dark-eyed wanderers of the pore blood. With George Borrow (continued the writer) I love the Gipsy, and although he takes toll now and again of the land- owner's partridges and the farmer's rabbits, and sometime', but more rarely, appropriates the cottager', foals, on the whole he is more law-abiding and lees quarrelsome than his Er.glish imitator and incomparably more sober in his habits. But soon the c,tintry lanes will know him no more." " FELOBES JACK."

I always read with interest " Uncle Caleb's " paragraphs for the children ; but is him last week's reference to " Petorn. Jack "quite up-to-date ? Ile I seems to write of it on the Resumption that this world- famoue and most intelligent monster of the deep welts still piloting New Zealand-bound vessels into Pelorus Sound ; but! eomewhere read a few weeka ago that it had disappeared and was presumed to be dead. I have been trying to find the item, but failed to lay my hands upon it. However, lam sure " I'ado Caleb" will not mind my mentioning the matter here. VENICE.

"Uncle's" allusion to the Bridge of Sighs not only sent me back to the darn of my boyhood when I revelled in such stories as "The Bravo," but remiwiled rue of an Tmuming account of an Easter trip to Venice which a neighbour who joined a party of Cook's tourists gave me a few days ago. Be is what is usually described as • self-made nine, and boa not yet travelled much, so that he is still—well, a sort of diamond in the rough, and it is refreshing to haven chat with him Said he of Venice: "It was coming on dark when we got there, and they took us to th' hotel in gondolas. There wee four on us one., beside t' bloomin' foreigner 'at had charge on us. We didn't exactly like th' look ort him, an' when he turned down a ginnel, an' we lost th' sight o' t' others, we began to be a bit feared—l mean th' women did. It turned out 'at they were taking us th back road on, 'cos next morning when we walked out o' th' front door we was on St. Mark's Square. But, an deary me, Meows 2ititiefs ! I didn't make much o' new—that is, my wife an' t' other women didn't, 'speshly th' dark." Es+. raly, be had been reading Fennunore Cooper, too. ANONYMITY.

Of course I am not going to attempt to re-open the editorially closed coon...seamy respecting living statuary, but perhaps I may be permitted on general ' grounds to protest against the closing sentence in Mr. Georg! Smith's letter of a week ago. That doughty champion, preferring to write over his own proper !signature, calls upon an opponent to" throw aside the cloak of anonymity." It is an old device,and I venture to suggest that it is as a rule unfair. Let me make the position plain, for I am naturally anxious not to be misunderstood. Not long ago there was buried at Tunetall, S tran named leech, who according to his clergyman was literally killed by an anonymous letter writer. Leech received an anonymous letter Inflecting that he was a scoundrel. This was absolutely untrue, but Leech, a very sensitive man, felt the allegation so deeply that he took to his bed and died of a broken heart. As to this kind of thing I agree with • colleague who declares that the anonymous defamer is a coward and a villain all in one. Ile is a secret foe, who has not the manliness to "fight in the open." Ile prefers the method. of the asissein, a stab in the dark. He often does a fast amount of injury. All this being as a matter of course granted, I ask why anyone who may have a perfectly honour- able and legitimate reason for not wilting to disclose his identity (there is still, for insfance, some modesty in the world) should not be at liberty to discuss over a pen-name naattera of public interest without being suspected of base ulterior motives, or laying himself open to unworthy insinuations ? What about the anonymity of leader-writers for the Press? As the "Academy' onco well put it, working behind the invisible forces of our time there is a regiment of namelesa men who, refusing to fall in with the modern love of advertiminent, nevertheless exert an immeasurable influence upon their contempories They are birds of the night. When streets are hushed beneath the stars and the sober citizen ie asleep, they are toiling through " flimsy " and preparing opinions to guide the world at its awaking. But the/ cling to anonymity, and make their journal what the State was to the antique Roman citizen. They may see them- selves quoted but it is always as the paper, never by their own names. Mr. George Smith would not dream of calling to account the editor of the Examiner" becairm he does not sign his articles ; neither would he he so foolish as to question the good taste of the many old authors whom earlier books now accepted an CIASSieli, were published anonymously or the bona fides of a modern writer who chose in a first book to imitate them. Why, then, so long sake confines himself to the subject under consideration and avoids personalities, should not the ordinary newspaper correspondent be able to crows swords with another in relation even to living statuary without hie adversary begging the question and seeking refuge behind that ancient and well-afore and futile tiles into which in a moment of unwonted weeltnev s Mr. George Smith seems to me to have suffered himself to be betrayed?

div.head: iIRISH AFFAIRS. 1 NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
div.p: iIRISH AFFAIRS. 1 NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
VET) BILL THROUGH.

By the splendid majority of 121, and amid the enthusiastic cheer, of its supporters, the Veto Bill Passed its third reading in the House of Common. on Monday night hut. To the democratic and progressive ranks in the whole of the United Kingdom, there will not be wanting an apprecintion of the full significance of that piece of important political history. Certainly in Ireland and amongst the Irish here in Great Britain and abroad, &re exists the deeperst eatiafaction. And one of the chief reasons for that satisfaction is the thoroughneas which the Government is evincing in its determination to carry the N'eto Bill word for word to the steps of the throne. The debate, it will be recalled, was wound up by the Home Secretary in a speeds of immense power and brilliance, reiterating thy demand put forward earlier in the evening by the Prime klini.ter and by Lord Morley in the HMSO of Lords, that the whole Bill and nothing hut the Bill shall be passed into law. Mr. Churchill's statrinent was in reply to counsels of com- promise from Mr. Wal'er Long, and the fighting attitude shown in the speech has therefore a special vistnificance. The next point of gratification to the frith in that the staunch attendance of their members throughout all the tiresome and weary debates on the Veto Bill has contributed invaluably to the NUMMIX of the Government and that part of the King's dominions which has admittedly eufferel more than any other from the domination of autocracy has not been wanting in its supply of men and ammunition in this historic smash of feudal power.

SIR EDWARD CARSON AND HOME RULE. Sir Edward Carson in doing his best in his own war to excite feeling in England against Home Rule, and that he does not find the tank easy of accomplish- ment is shown by the sort of assertions to which he is driven. Speaking the other day at Runcorn, be revived the hackneyed and exploded theory that nothing was .aid of Home Rule by Ministers before the elections. A specimen of bin sarcasm is seen in his remark that be " could imagine Mr. Asquith explaining it away by saving that he had mentioned it about two years before in the Albert Hall." We have not space here to enumerate the occa,•ions on which Mr. Asquith pledged himself in the clearest terms, to introduce • Home Rule Bill—such an enumeration may be consulted by en, ne curious on the point in the column of the " Westminster (lazette." Had Sir Edward Carson said 'two days before the election " instead of "two years " he would have been accurate. Accuracy evidently it not that gentleman's strong point—but the surprising thing to us is that it la possible to get together an audience anywhere in England to whom it is posaible to make such manifest ruisrepre- eentations.

div.head: IRELAND AND THE INSURANCE SCHEME,
div.p: IRELAND AND THE INSURANCE SCHEME,

The explanatory memorandum issued in connection with Mr. Lloyd George's gigmtic insurance scheme serves to emphasise the importance and the difficulty of the task involved by consideration of this measure in relation to Ireland. 'Fbe duty of close examination rests upon employers and worker alike, and in a special degree upon County Councils, which are expected to bear an onerous part in the administra- tion of the measnre. The clauses dealing with the application of the Bill to Ireland, raise in concrete form some of the oneetions which most be discussed by representative bylies, by employers and by workpenple—and more especially those of the latter who are connected with Friendly Societie.. The most important exceptioa referring to dd. country is concerned with the numerical strength of • society to be deemed an "approved society." With regard to Great Britain the minimum membership is 10,000 ; it is to be enacted that ball the number will suffice in the case of Ireland, should the Insurance Commissioner. approve. The cause illustrates the Be ions character of the obligation which the Councils are expected to discharge. Generally the administ on of the sickness fund will be in the hands of Conn Health Committees, • third of whose membership will be drawn from the County Councils, end if the Health Committee he anxious to spend more money than it has at its disposal upon medical and ranatorimn needs the County Councils have power " as the Chancellor puts it "to sanction further expenditure, provided that the Treasury also agree--one half of the additional expenditure, to conic out of the rates and the other half out of the treasury." The County Councillors have a further task—though not obligatory--i.e , the submitting of a echeme to the Insurance Commissioners for the establishment of • Ceunty Society, to embrams employed contributors eho are not members of any society. It sill be seen, therefore, that both in book- keeping details and general constructive policy, • good deal is looked for from the busy people who form the Irish County Councils.

When Mr. Redmond, on behalf of the Irish people and the lush part..., wisely entered a "caveat" in respect of this huge scheme the provisions relating to Ireland had not been stated. The publicstion of them since should give a stimulus to the inquiry advised by Mr. Redmond. Sympathising perhaps moreaeenly than any other party leader since unfor- tunately the Irish people contain more of the very poor than the rest of the people of these islands, it is nevertheless to be noted that his caution was enjoined by experience of mazy British mea‘ures well adapted for British needs hut conceived and drafted without regard to Irish conditions. Looking upon Mr. Lloyd ileorge's proposals not as a graceful offering from Fairyland, but as a business proposition, it would memo that in Ireland the rinerition that swill have to be put and examined is how will this scheme work out in a country where industries are few, small, and narrow in their profit margins. The investigation suggested by Mr. Itedmonde caveat •hould be under- taken at once, and the Irish Leader has commenced himself by despatching copim of the Bill to the chair- men and secretaries of all the County Councils and County Borough Councils of Ireland.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MAY ID MU.

Mr. LLOYD GEORGE'S A GREAT Budget spen'a had BUDGEr. decided points of originality. There were no flourishes in it. The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER was concerned almost solely with what he had to say to the House snd the nation, and scarcely at all with the manner of saying it. We know how interestingly he could have played with his subject if he had chosen to do so, and what charming passages might have been introduced into the speech if he had occupied three hours instead of about half that time. But no oratorical triumphs could have been quite so effective as his actual plainness of statement. No previous Chancellor of the Exchequer has ever presented to the House of Commons a Budget resembling even remotely that which was unfolded in so businesslike a manner on Tuesday. The facto seemed too massive for any sort of ornamentation. The present year's Budget will be not less historic than that of Mr. GLaDsToNE's in 1853. But it is on simple, broad, commanding lines. It has no complexities, and Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE presented it with as little parade as if he were a sculptor unveiling his work before his critics.

The sums dealt with are, of course, immense. Even the most economical Govern- ment must accomodate itself to an increas- ing expenditure. The State is doing much more than it did, and therefore it has to pay much more than it did. Take some new items of expenditure. For example, old age pensions are to cost betweeen 12 and 13 mil- lions. A million and half is to go to road development, and the same sum to the estab- lishment of sanatoria. Payment of members of Parliament is to cost a quarter of a million and national insurance will carry off another £50,000. Here we have as unaccustomed liabilities what was more than one third of the national income from sixty to seventy years ago. But on the top of this we have a Naval expenditure of over £44,000,000 and our Army expenditure in proportion. The other services are increasing in costliness. Post Office expenses, for instance, are up by a million and a-quarter. Added to this,there has not yet been a complete recovery from the " consequences "of which Lord MILNER was so scornful two years since. Yet there is no new call on the taxpayer. On the contrary, there is some relief to taxation. All that can properly be described as "pro- tective" in the cocoa duties is to disappear. There are reductions on account of liquor licences involving a loss of .£50,000 a year. Another reduction concerns stamps on short- dated securities.

Such are the splendid results of Free Trade finance. And there are more to follow. The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER has been fiercely attacked from the Opposition side of the House and in the Tory Press on the ground that he has not acted fairly by the Sinking Fund. It will be noted with interest, therefore, that to what is known as the old sinking fund he devotes more than two millions and a quarterof his realised surplus. This, however, gives no indication of the extent to which he has reduced the nation's debt. During this year alone, provision is

being made for the reduction of our capital liabilities by close on 12 millions. Since he has been CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER he has reduced these liabilities by £28,700,000. In three years Mr. ASQUITH paid off £42,000,000 of debt. Since it took up office, therefore, the present Administration has paid off debts to the extent of £7o,ooo,ooo.This is a unique achievement. Mr. GLADSTONE mever equalled it. The saving to the tax- payer is a sum of £2,000,000 a year.

The problem of the payment of members is -simply and effectively solved by the Budget. It is solved without the imposition of a penny of taxation. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE shoulders the new burden in his stride. The amount lo be paid to each member of the House of Commons is £4OO. This is neither extrava- gant nor penurious It has been suggested that rich members will decline to take the money on their own behalf, but will present it to their own constituencies. That is a con- -tingency that will certainly be guarded against. The bribing of constituences with public money is something that will not be permitted. Generally, the Budget is so remarkable, it is so bold, and at the same time so unpretentious, that praise is uncalled for and superfluous.

The third annual SCHOOL HYGIENE, report of the Medical Officer on school hygiene possesses many features which call for the serious attention of the Education and Health authorities, and it would be a wise plan to carry out the suggestion of the Chairman of the Education Committee and hold a special meeting to consider the report in detail. Dr. Hibbert again alludes to the many structural defects of the older schools, and the want of endeavour to remedy the faults. No less than 5,103 children were medically examined during the year, and many children's ailments of a preventible nature found to be common. The percentage of children with verminous heads was 413, the girls, by reason of their longer hair, being the chief sufferers. Hair cut for boys, and plaits for girls, are simple remedies. Boots, shoes, and garments in many cases testified to neglectful mothers. In a smaller proportion more serious cases of physical defect or weakness were discovered, 173 requiring medical treatment for which special provision is now made under the school clinic. None but the best results can be anticipated as a result of the increasing concern of the authorities for the physical welfare,as well as the mental development, of the thousands of children under their charge and every encouragement should be given to the raising of school hygiene to a foremost place in educational administration.

All the prophecies of FREE TRADE Tariff Reformers that SUNSHINE. our trade was being captured by foreign .countries, and of Tories that a democratic Budget would kill industry by driving capital abroad, have been rigidly falsified. A trade boom set in in 1909 and has been in-progress ever since. In the last three months there has been a gratifying rise in home 'lway securities. The Bankers' Clearinghouse returns beat all records. But electors must not forget, in this bright sunshine, that the Tariff Reformer is still hovering on the , horizon, like a vulture seeking for a corpse to devour, and that he is only waiting for a black background "—if some international crisis of finance or other accidental blow to national prosperity should arise—upon which to project his delusive scheme and lure the country into ruin.

Out of the confused and POOR LORD conflicting voices which LANsnowNE. have been heard this week in the gilded Chamber across the Lobby from the great elective assembly of the nation—that Chamber which, by an anachronism is still called the Upper House "—two utterances seem to male themselves heard with special distinct- ness. There is Lord Lansdowne confessing that his " Reform " Bill does not solve the main problem of the relation between the two Houses; and there is the Duke of Northumberland declaring that democracy is only a symptom of national decadence, and that the business of the statesman is to curb and check democracy. Lord Lansdowne, like Moses between the dead and the living, or the ancient Latin God, Janus, who looked two ways at once, finds his time fully occu- pied telling the democracy that the House of Lords is going to carry out the will of the people even more thoroughly than the House of Commons, and telling the backwoodsmen that it is "all right, the democracy are going to be dished." Poor Lord Lansdowne!

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

No exaggeration has been used to picture the charm and beauty of the performance at the Palace and Hippodrome this week which has for its centre of attraction Little Elise Craven, the child-dancer who created such a furore in London in " Pinkie and the , Fairies." "There is no grace that doth not cling about" little Elite. She is a wonderful dancer, a consummate artiste, and a delighful young person. In "The King's High-road" she has an admirable setting for romance and art. As Barbara Barrington (a dancer) she is held up on the Heath by the bold highwayman, who eventually succumbs to her fascinations and the wonder of a pas eetirfit for Royal favour which *lle dances on the greensward. Mr. Charles Cautley makes a capital " Jack o' the Heath." and sings and dances with the little fairy in charming fashion. Enthusiastic applaum is the due toned of both, and they get it in full meas- ure. The rest of the bill this week, is up to the highest standard, and one does not recall a better variety entertainment in Warrington for a long time back. Kenna Brothers, the aviators, provide a screamingly funny acrobatic mid-air turn, and are certainly in stage ahead of most competitors in their line of muscle and mirth com- bined. Quite a novel scene is that entitled "On the Farm," wherein Leon and Tee (who differ in sex) harmonise quaintly in music and mimicry. The farmyard area, is full of detail and humorous invention, and the whole turn appeals to the fun-loving side of a music-hall audience. Marie Kay distinguishes herself in the role of soubrette and dancer, and some fine combined and solo singing is heard from the accomplished Landis Trio of °politic vocalists. The diminutive Cambia is one of the cleverest tumblers and sleight of hand experts on the boards, and his continental specialities, including a complete somersault on one leg " fetch" the audience every time. Barry Eldon is a comedienne with a pleasing manner and sumo good songs, and Harley and Melton excel in boisterous crone-talk and ecentric dancing. The music throughout the even- ing is excep:ionally pleasing, and the Perfection Pictures live up to their name.

Viscount Haldane, Secretary for War, in opening a new drill hall at Ipswich, on Satur- day said that the Territorial Army had come to stay, and as an educative and patriotic institution should grow stronger and an increasingly useful force as time went on. • •

The Lancashire, Cheshire and North- Western Liberal Federation will, on Friday evening, the 16th June, entertain the Right Hon. Sir John Brunner, Bart„ President of the Federation, to a complimentary dinner, in recognition of his long and valuable services to Liberalism. The Right Hon, Lord Shuttleworth, a vice-president of the Federation, will be the chairman of the gathering, which will be held in the Reform Club, Manchester. The arrangements are in the hands of the Executive Committee of the Federation, and any inquiries will be gladly received by the secretary of the Federation, 37, Cross-street, Manchester.
The thunderstorm of Saturday last seems to have been the most erratic of its kind. In some

parts of the Warrington area serious damage wasdone by lightning, streets were absolutely flooded, and the electricity of the atmosphere proved too much for that of the Corporation, with the result that the car service was stopped. At various points of the borough boundary not enough rain fell to wet the parched gardens. Burnley received the visitation a little later, and even more severely than Warrington, and in five hours on Saturday and Sunday, no less than three inches of rain fell.

• • • The Guilds of Help of the country have been conferring at Birmingham this week to practical purpose. Among many important topics discussed was that of" Mutual Regis- tration of Assistance," which is designed to prevent the work of the numerous charity organisations over-lapping and consequently losing much of its value. True co-operation instead of a certain amount of aloofness, between these various bodies, is the greatest essential toeffteient charitable and ameliora- tive effort. If the Guilds of Help only succeed in linking the arms of their pre- decessors with their own, they will have made a great advance towards the achieve- ment of their high ideal. „ .

The whacking of. the small-boy is frequently necessary, and we have con- siderable sympathy with the Warburton schoolmaster who was fined at Lymm on Wednesday for a technical assault. Two boys, out of school, seem to have indulged in the pleasant pastime of deriding the authority of a master, and when caught and spanked they appealed to the law. The law, being a "bass," had to convict the master for administering a correction which was entirely for the public good. There is only one way of dealing effectively with the small-boy in the mannerless cub stage, and unfortunately the legislature does not recognise the fact or .the remedy.

A trophy for annual competition among affiliated miniature rifle clubs, Territorial battalions, lads' brigades, and boy scouts, in the county of Lancashire is offered by Lord Shuttleworth, the Lord Lieutenant and will be open to teams of six each. The trophy is vested in the Liverpool Miniature Rifle Association, and it is proposed to divide the county into districts, the winning teams in each being drawn against each other until the semi-final round. The ranges will be from 25 to 100 yards. In presenting this trophy Lord Shuttleworth expresses the earnest hope that it may encourage members of the Territorial forces to join miniature rifle clubs, to which may be added the hope that rifle clubs may send more recruits to the ranks of the Territorials.

• • As the result of a visit to her uncle, Lord Gladstone, of Cape Town, news comes of the engagement of Miss Dorothy Drew to Captain Parish, one of his Excellency's A.D.C.'s. The marriage will not take place until next year, as Miss Drew is only 20,and the only child of her widowed mother. Mrs. Drew and her sister, Miss Helen Gladstone, are accompanying Miss Drew on her visit to South Africa. They are now at Pretoria, but they will return to London next month. Miss Drew was the favourite grandchild and companion of the late Mr. Gladstone, with whom she spent the early years of her life. As a child she was frequently photographed with him in his library and in the gardens and park at Hawarden. Captain Parish is a nephew of Lady Shuttleworth, and a grand- son of the late Sir Woodbine Parish.

• • It is a strange anomaly that children's education should suffer as the sobriety of the people increases. The Cheshire Education Committee has been bemoaning the loss of £15,000 revenue previously derived from whiskey-money, and Low not forthcoming from this source owing to the decline in the consumption of whiskey. A hoarse and menacing growl has made itself heard in the right quarter, and this week the chairman of the Cheshire Education Committee was able to announce with satisfaction that the Chancellor of the Exchequer had consented to make good the deficiency. What a wonderful Chancellor he is who can reduce the whisky-drinking of the people, and yet find the revenue to supply all deficiencies—to say nothing of providing old-age pensions and state insur- ance for the poor, and £4OO a year for M.P.'s.

The proposal contained in the Reform Bill of the Marquis of Lansdowne that Peers of the Realm who are not of necessity Peers of Parliament should be permitted to stand for the House of Commons will recall an amus- ing controversy which happened a few years ago when .the present Earl_ of Selborne,

Viscount Midletan and Lord Curzon headed a revolt against the compulsory transference of the eldest sons of Peers to the Upper Chamber on the death of their fathers. The contention which they advanced (says the " Daily News") was that a Peer of the Realm was not necessarily a Peer of Parliament, and therefore it was not incumbent upon them to quit the seats which they had occupied in the Commons. The expedient which they proposed to adopt was simply to take no steps whatever to assert their right to a seat in the Gilded Chamber. When the present Lord Selborne, at the time Viscount Wohner, succeeded to the earldom he endeavoured to assert this right by taking his seat in the Commons next to his leader, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, but he was not destined to remain for long unobserved, as Mr. Labouchere was quick to
detect the presence of a stranger within the Parliamentary precincts, and the intruder was promptly ordered by the Speaker to withdraw below the Bar.

By the mere pressing of a button King George was enabled to unveil the Queen Victoria Memorial on Wednesday—go thoroughly has electricity been.harnessed to man's use nowadays. By far the most remarkable ceremony of this nature was performed by the late King Edward in October 1909, when, by operating a small switch placed in Buckingham Palace, he opened the doors of a newly erected hospital in Montreal. This one action of King Edward also lit myriads of electric lights in Montreal and hoisted a flag on the roof of the hospital.

Suicide at Howley. At the l'olue Station, on Thursday, Mr. S Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on Thomas Ford, We cutter, GI years of age, 33, Howley-lane, who committed suicide by hanging himself. Ellen Ford, disease's wife, stated that at 7.30 on Wednes- day morning her married daughter, Amelia Howard, came upstairs and told her there was a man in the pantry. On going downstairs she found deceased hanging by a scarf from a nail over the pustry do x. A man named George Thornley cut him down, but life was extinct on the arrival of Dr. Anderson. Deceased had been away from work for • fortnight owing to ill health and on Tuesday he complained of pains in the head and that his eyes were aching.— A verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was returned.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.

Wrecker of lien." , Mr. C. Watson Mills drama "A wrecker of men,"' which is being played at the Royal Court Theatre this week, has undoubtedly the merit of originality. Escapes from prison and shipwiecks, which help to make up the list of sensatiot fl, ate fairly familiar to the theatre habitue but in the last Oct we hare some- , thing entirely new. hi-ca }Jellison, a modern ' Delilah who takes a fiendish delight in blighting the happiness of men, is taken to the mysterious temple of Karnach in Egypt and there meets with terrible I retribution, being smitten with blindness by a wrath- ful goddess. The play is based on the idea of reincarnation which is held to account for the inhuman callousness of the woman who lures men to ruin. The unattractive role of lilacs Ileitis m is rery cleverly portrayed by Alias Ruth Shepherd who is an actress of superior talents and never over-does her part. Mr. Arthur S. Pitt, as that rough diamond Jitn Morley, quickly gains the favour of the audience by a vigorous and thoroughly realistic impersonation t f the much-abused convict. Mr. Reginald Garland is particularly good as the wily Egyptian wanderer and the various subsidiary parts ate well sustained. • NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. , Next week Max Goldberg's comedy sporting drama " Rogues of the turf " will be presented and should prove a great attraction. Although largely concerned with the race course, the play has a strong ganaral interest and there isa rich fund of comedy. Three thoroughbred race: horses will play their part in the last act which concludes with the great race for the Manchester cup.

div.head: PROSPECTIVE PEERS.
div.p: PROSPECTIVE PEERS.
MR CROSFIELD IN THE LIST.
Men Whose Votes May Carry the Veto Bill.

Reynolds Newspaper.' (published yester- ) says :—There are again rumours that the peers intend to reject the Veto Bill in foto. In best informed circles, however, it is not thought likely that they will adopt such an insane and reckless policy. Ths Govern- ment are determined that the Veto Bill shall become law, and thus put an end once and for all to the spurious contention that the House of Lords have a constitutional and legitimate right to exercise a control over the financial policy of the country. It is, of course, possible that the peers will, in their blindness, risk another collision with the people's representatives. In this case it is certain the Government will exercise their , right to create a. sufficient number of peers to enable them to place the Veto Bill on the Statute Book.

We give herewith a first list of some 250 gentlemen who, it is understood, are on the first list of stalwarts who will be offered the honour of helping to make history by accept- ing seats in the House of Lords"
The list includes Sir John Brunner, Bart., ex-M.P. for Nantwich. Mr. A. H. Warrington. Sir W. J. Crossley, Bart., ex-M.P. for Al trincham,

div.head: PHYLLOXERA IN AUSTRALIA.
div.p: PHYLLOXERA IN AUSTRALIA.

The increasing prices of the better type of Australian I wines is due to the vine-scourge which has affected ; many of the vineyards, las: as the extensive wine- making districts of the continent were stricken a few years ago. The parasitic insect phylloxera by its rout-attache cantles the leaves of the vines to blacken and the grape. to shrivel, and wine made from such berries acquires a curious taste, is not easy of digestion, and should be avoided. These affected wines are still bought and at low prices, but firms of repute, jealous of tleir reputation for fair dealing, avoid their sale. Higbee prices must sow be psid for the lees expensive gradesof Australian wine to Nance floe and sound quality, as their production daring rawest vintages I. sadly reduced. During the last five years the vintage of Australia has decreased by almost one half, but the strenuous efforts of those concerned portends a brighter future.

div.head: MR. W. P. RYLANDS GIVES THE TARIFF REFORM CASE
div.p: MR. W. P. RYLANDS GIVES THE TARIFF REFORM CASE
How the Consumer Pays.

In discussing the State Insurance Scheme in the columns of our contemporary last Saturday, Mr. W. P. Rylands made a remarkable admission, which was probably involuntary, but none the less striking on that account. He was arguing that the cost of State insurance would be an additional burden to the manufacturer, and an "added premium to our foreign competitors." What did Germany do, under very similar conditions?
1 This is Mr. Rylands' illuminating explipa- tion :

"In Germany, the State, by a system of import duties, enables the manufac- turers to place the burden upon the home consumers as a whole, and in return for this advantage the manufac- turers are well content to pay the price." The italics are ours, but the words Atre Mr. Rylands' _ _

Even in Germany—that el Dorado of ' Protection—Mr. Rylands tells us that 'a system of import duties enables the manu- facturers to place the burden upon the home consumers." In Warrington, England, Mr. IRylands and his political associates have impressed upon us,—oh sooften!—that import duties make the foreigner pay. "Tax the foreigner" has b-en the cry of the ardent Tariff Reformer. Put duties on the goods which he is treacherously sending here to compete with the home-made article and make him pay! Retaliation and the big revolver I A glorious policy, ha hail Meanwhile we Free Traders emphasised the point that the duties would redound on the buyer, and not on the seller, in the long run. We should merely be taxing ourselves and not the foreigner. Preposterous l—suoth the Tariff Reformers. Make the foreigner pay, pay, pay I ! I . . _ .

Arid iinCv Mr. Rylands comes along with the statement that, after all, it is the home consumer who pays and not the foreigner, by a system of import duties. He adds, too, with refreshing simplicity, that the manu- facturer places the burden on the consumer— (we said he would I)—and is well content to pay the price. Perfidious manufacturer I ! The truth is out at last, but we wish Mr. Rylands had spoken in this strain a few years earlier. He would have saved such a lot of that dreary drip of monotonous reiteration which both sides to the fiscal controversy were obliged to indulge in or be talked out. Yet, even now, Mr. Ryland* being a manufacturer we suppose he will still swear by import duties as the panacea for all the ills the nation is heir to. But he cannot any more deny that THE CON- SUMER PAYS, even if he should be indifferent to the fact.
Tariff Reform had its eighth birthday this week. Mr. Rylands has celebrated the occasion in fitting style. Like Lord Lans- downe he has given the coup-de-grace to his nearest and dearest!

div.p: HOW TO BE WELL, THOUGH AGED.

Though seventy years of age Mrs. Jane Elizabeth Sharpe is mentally and physically as fit to-day as many people twenty years younger. Seated in her cosy quarter. at 2, Harrison's Hoapital, Hull, she related recently how she bas managed to preserve bee health and youthful vigour no " Yea, I am very well and happy." she said, th. ugh I have panned through many troubles--the worst, perhaps, about five years ago. My health fell away very quickly, and a good deal of dizziness troubled me. My 'food did not nourish me, and I never felt one bit better for anything I took. For hours every night I could not sleep, and all through the day I was exhausted for want of rest at nights." The interviewer gathered that with advancing years the attacks of dizziness became more general and that actual collapses frequently took place. One day in particular, Mrs. Sharpe had cause to remember, for while walking in the street the fell helpless into a doorway, and those who came to her assistance thought idle wee dead. Ever since its erection in 1A7(), the church has been in charge of the Rev. Th.. Byrn Williamson, B.A„whnse quiet yet diligent and fruitful work is much appreciated by his flock, lie was born sixtyreight years ago in the Cleveland district of Yorkshire, and come, of a long line of parsons. Having received his early education at Mailliorongh College, he proceeded to Jesus College, Cambridge. where he took the degree of BA, in lAfif. listens ordained deacon in 1817 by the Bishop of Chester and priest in Igeo: by the Bishop of Litchfield. div.head: SHUNTING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SHUNTING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
Wagons Derailed and Shunter Killed.

An inquest was held et the Warrington Police Station on Thursday by Mr. S. Ilrighonee, County Coroner, concerning the desth of Albert Enron, a shunter, 33 years of age, of G, liarnard-street, who was killed on Tuesday et the works of Metiers. Monks, Ilall and Co., Liverpool-road, where he had been employed for fifteen years. Mr. F. 0. Tsylor, solicitor, appeared for the firm, Mr. T. S. Steel for the relative., and Mr. Warren. factory inspector, was also present. The evidence showed that the deceased was engaged in shunting • number of wagons laden with iron rods. The wagons preceded the engine, and the deceased we seen riding on one of the buffer,' of the foremost wagon. The wagon fouled the point., with the result two wagons were derailed, and the decessed either jamped off or was thrown under the wagons. Ile was found in dying condition under the second wegonAnd he succumbed to his injuries before the ambulance arrived.. . . .

—Ti,;-(-2.oroner pointed out that there was a regulation under the Factory net Workshops Act, that no person shall be upon the buffer of a locomotive or vragon in motion, unless there is a secure hand-hold," __

—danl;n•ltimrner, foreman ya-rd laboure-r, 33, 'leak.), street, said the train was travelling at seven or eight miles an hour. Ile had very rarely seen a man riding on the buffer of a wagon. A juror remarked that it would bare been impossible fee deceased to walk •loagaide the wagons, as there was scrap metal piled apes. each side of the line. Samuel Webster, foreman shooter, 12 Rostock-street, prefaced his evidence with the remark " I am a foreman for taking and giving orders, but 1 have no power." (Laughter). The Coroner : You seem to be apprehensive. Don't try to play the old soldier with us. We are very cute. (Caught.. Witness stated that his estimate of the speed was flve mil. an hour. Witness was standing in the fourth wagon and deceased was standing in the drst when he passed on the signal to wit..s, which he in turn transferred to the driver. He waa certain deceased awn standing in the wagon and notes the huller. ..

e • In answer to Mr. Star/ witness said he knew there eras a Factory Act regulation to the effect that where- ever it was safe end practicable a man should precede the frost wagon or other sufficient marine should be taken to obviate risk of accident. Ile admitted that it would be difficult for deceased to keep in front of a train which was travelling at five miles an hour. David Harris, traffic manager, mid berme, the deceased sitting on the buffer smi called out to him that be was in a dangerous poaition. Deceased replied' All right ; someone hen got lode it." Deceased was disobeying the regulations. AN there were only very low eider to the wagon it was possible that ,lecenved cont./ have been standing in the waggon when Webster saw him and afterwards got on to the buffer while the train was in motion.
: It wan an inipossibility for deceased to heve carried out the regulations to walk in front of the train and in eight of the driver. Ile could, however, have stood on sn elevation near the line.

The Coroner said that ws 4Oft. rode were projecting over the wagon, the buffer might have been as Rafe a place as any other for the deceased to occupy. The jury returned a verdict of Accidental death," adding that there wee no blame attached to the ' employer, or the deceased. Mr. Taylor expressed sympathy with the relatives on behalf of the company.

div.head: St. Barnabas' Church. Dedication of the New Organ.
div.p: St. Barnabas' Church. Dedication of the New Organ.
Vs

A service which had been looked forward to a itls great interest by the congregation of St. !inrushes' Church took place on Tuesday evening when the Ten. Archdeacon Spooner dedicated the organ recently installed eta cost of £450. Although it waa a beauti• fully floe evening, the church wan well filled, and the proceedings were of an impressive character befitting such a red letter occasion in the history of the parish. The actual dedication ceremony was very brief. Immediately the clergy and choir had taken their places Archdeacon Spooner, standing near the organ, offered special prayers in which the instrument was solemnly set apart for purpose. of Divine worship. Choral F,vensong followed, the organ being played with taste and skill by Mr. F. M. Darby, Mn.. liacs, organist of the Warrington Parish Church. The prayers were intoned by the Rev. J W. Glendenning, of Holy Trinity, Wavertree (formerly curate at St. !tarnishes') and the lemons read by the Rev. J. H. Ci. liollingworth (vicar, and the Rev. J. It Jones ,vicar of Great Sankey).

Archdeacon SeriONYR preached an appropriate sermon from the words " Praise ye the Lord " ,Psalm vi., 6,. It bad been Plaid, he pointed out, that there were two great defector in the religious life of modern times, the one being that there was not sufficient room, scope or opportunity given for meditation, and the other that we were too forgetfol of God'e claim upon as in the matter of adoration. That night be wanted to direct their thoughts along the line auggeeted by the words of the text—that of praise. Spanking of the praise of God in nature, the preacher said that three who had etudied carer illy the Psalms and the prophetical writings, would have noticed what • close connection there•seerned to be between the prophets ant the p•almi•ta and nature—a sort of secret understand- ing end mystical indea of sympathy between the two. If we were to enter into the prairie. aspect of nature, there must be the same kindrep spirit. Our Lord Josue Christ took some of His most beautiful illustrations for the enforcement of spiritual truth from the hook of nature which mac so widely opened all around Him in His native land. It was not mere trentiment or emotionalism but • grand truth that the voices of nature were bearing their tribute of Praise to Almighty God. Not only must there be a kinship and sympathy between us and nature. but we should see that nature praised God in the fultihnent of those laws which God had impressed upon nature's bi•ng. flow often, if we could only feel and appreciate it, did we stand rebuked by the various phenomena in nature. They were obeying God's laws, and yet how often we who bore the name of Jeans Christ and who claimed to be the children of (iod not only by creation bat in the higher sense by adoption and grace, were wetting et defiance His law, sod forgetting the words "if ye love Me, keep My commandrnenta; Passing on to consider the position and relationship of praise in public worship, the preacher said • great change had come over the attitude of the Christian public towards the use of music in Church service.. He never could understand why at any time In the Church's history people should have been averse to the rise of music ss a medium of expressing their feelings of praise and thanksgiving to Almighty God. In connection with the place of instru- mental music in service, One or two points had to he borne in mind. The purpose of the organ, for instance, was to accompany, and to sustain the singing of a con• gregation. not they bad to remember that the inter- pretation of music in the case of the organ depended very largely not only upon the proficiency of the organist, hut also upon tire reverent praise spirit which he poseesned. If he •ntered into the spirit of the service which he wee musically rendering ; if he felt that he was leading— and the remarks applied equally to the choir—the worship of Almighty God r and if he felt that he was consecrating the powers which God had given him in order that the eery'ce might be elevated, ennobled and ! made more worthy of God's acceptance, it would make all the difference to their feelings where the musical service was so rendered. Had they not sometimes, wben listening toan organ recital,felt that while the technique was perfect and no fault could be found with the render. ing of the music, so tarn. the note., were concerned, there sons nothing which had appealed to the deeper feelings' And in another case had they not listened end felt that the organises whole soul went out with what he WAR playing—that he wan enreptared in the Muller piece he was trying to Interpret !The organ seemed to speak to them in it. wonderful composition in a variety of ways. The preacher then emphasised the spiritual truths which the various organs comprised in one instrument might be said to symbolise. Ile also remembered that the organ he had just dedicated was a very beentifol one, •drnirably constructed. and judging from the •fforte of the con- gregation, he doubted not that in a short time it would he completed by the addition of the choir organ. Laetly. let them not forget that they were called upon to praise God in their being, character, and in their livers. Epeaking of the consecration of the intellect to the service of God, the preacher mil the mind was often vitiated by the reading of unwholesome

literature. If. did not condemn the proper novvl many of the novels of the present day were slant lag and instructive and set able characters before to as exempla—but be was afraid a great deal of the litera- ture found not only in the larkingran'a cottage but on the drawing-room table of the palace wa not,either in the reading or in the writing of it. a praising of God. div.p: PICTURES OF THE WEEK.

THE UNVEILING OF THE ViCTORIA MEMORIAL BY THE KING. The ceremony of 113 V( fling he National Memorial to Queen Victoria was performed on Tuesday by King George in the presence of a - large gathering of Royal Personages, which included, in addition to Queen Mary, the German Emperor and Empress, old Princess Victoria of Prussia, the Princess Royal, and the Duke of Connaught. The Memorial has occupied Mr. Thomas Brock, R.A. since 1902, when King Edward approved the d.sign. The base was completed and opened to the public two years ago, the erection of the central part being begun in the latter part of 1907. The marble used is of the finest quality, and upwards of two thousand tons hive been incor- porated in the work, whilst about eight hundred tons of the finest Aberdeen granite have been used in the structure of two flights of steps and the plateau. Tl.e central feature of the monument rises to a heght of 82 feet, and the statue of Queen Victoria, which is shown in the centre of the picMre, is 18 feet in height. His Majesty conferred the honour of Knighthood on Mr. Brock, R.A., the designer and sculptor of the Memorial. Our picture shows the actiLit unveiling, with ihe drapery tatting away from the figure of Q 1.14011 Victoria.

THE CROWN PRINCE AND PRINCESS OF GERMANY. The Crown Prince and Princess, who are to visit this country as representatives of the Kaiser at the Coronation, have lately returned from an extensive tour in the Near East, which included a Cate visit to India and Egypt. The Crown Prince and Princess enjoy the reputation of being more in love with each other than any other Royal couple in the world. Since their marriage the Princess has made her influence very much felt at the German Court. and is immensely popular among the people. She is also a housewife quite after the German pattern, and is devoted to her two sturdy little sons.

div.head: F") CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conductcd by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: F") CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conductcd by UNCLE CALEB.
THE ORANGE SECRET.
It was told me by Maritza, a little Greek girl in far-away Turkey, and I am going to tell it here and now to every one because I never have found an American child who bad discovered it.

I was finishing my breakfast one morn- ing when I heard a little sound at my elbow. It was Maritzs, who had slipped off her shoes at the outer door, and come so softly through the open hall that I had not beard her.

After I had taken the parcel of sewing her mother had sent, I gave Maritza two oranges which were left in a dish on the table. One of them was big and the other quite small. 'One orange is for you," I said, " and the other you may carry to Louka. Which one will you give him ?" Maritza waited a long while before answering. At any time she would have thought it rude for a little child to answer promptly or in a VOIC3 loud enough to be easily heard; but this time she waited even longer than good manners required. She looked one orange over and over, and then the other. After a little more urging from me, she whispered :—" This one." It was the big one. Curious to know of the struggle which made her so long in deciding, I said : " But why don't you give Louka the small orange? He is a small boy."
Maritza dug her little stockinged toes into the carpet and twisted her apron hem before she answered.

"Is not Anna waiting for me at the gate?" she said. " Anna and I will eat my orange together. Mine has twelve pieces, and the other only eleven. Anna would not like to take six pieces if! had only five." "You cannot see through the orange skin, Maritza, to tell how many pieces there are. Row is it you know ?" I asked. Then Maritza told me the orange secret, and this is it :

If you look at the stem-end of an orange you will see the scar where it was pulled away from the stem is like a little whoel,with spokes going out from the centre. If you count the spaces between these spokes you will find that there ere just as many of them se there will be sections in the orange when you open it: and so you can tell, as Maritza did, how many " pieces " your orange has. Perhaps you think every orange has the same number, just as every apple has five cells which hold its seeds; but you will find it is not so. Why not? Well, I do not know. But, perhaps away back in the history of the orange, when it is a flower, or perhaps when it is only a bud, something may happen which hurts some of the cells or makes some of them outgrew the rest. Then the number of cells is mixed; and no matter how pig and plump and juicy the orange becomes, it has no more sections than . .
it had when it Was a little green buCt.;:j.uei beginning to be an orange.
The next time you eat an orange, try to find out its secret before you open it.

Ours was always saying to sny husband, ' Yes, John,' and to me, ' Very well, Mary,' etc. So when roe got a new cook I told my husband to avoid calling me ' Mary,' RS then, not knowing my name, he would have to nay' mime ' tome. So John always called

nations sat at St. Helena, and the Prince do Joinville was officially authorized to receive the body on behalf of the French Govern- ment. There was considerable difficulty in getting out the coffin. When at length it could be opened it was found that the body was not in the least decomposed, the features were as firm and clear as. they had been in . . .

life,and the identification needea no collateral evidence to establish it. But had such evidence been needed, all was found as the old sergeant had said; the cocked hat was upon the breast, the sword packed close by the side, and the silver mug containing the heart placed between the legs. The coffin was re-soldered and carried off to France, where, as everyone knows, it found its permanent resting-place in the Hotel des Invalides, at Park.

div.head: IDENTIFICATION AT ST. HELENA FROM An An Interestiug Story Told by the Late LABOUR'S STANDPOINT. Rector 0 Warrington.
div.p: IDENTIFICATION AT ST. HELENA FROM An An Interestiug Story Told by the Late LABOUR'S STANDPOINT. Rector 0 Warrington.

The deepest interest still attaches to the wonderful personality of the first Napoleon, and every detail of his career is a subject of eager discussion. There will be many, Vierefore, who will be attracted by a narra- tive written by the late Rector of Warring- ton, the Rev. Wm. Quekett, which describes the last days and burial of the great soldier and Emperor. We give the story in Mr. Quekett's own words.

"'t'he French Government applied to the English Government in 1840 for the removal ' of Napoleon's body from St. Helena to France. In order that there might be no mistake as to the identity of the body, three Commis- sioners from each country were appointed to go to St. Helena and have the body disinterred.

I was one day visiting my brother, Professor Quekett, at the College of Surgeons, when I found him talking to'a gentleman in the Museum. After this gentleman had left him he asked if I knew who it was. On replying that I did not, my brother said that he was a noted member of the Collego of Physicians, who had been appointed by the Government to go to St. Helena for the identification of the body of Napoleon. He had expressed his sense of the difficulty of the Commission; for should decomposition have destroyed the features, there was really nothing that he knew of by which to certify the identity. I told my brother I knew how to identify the body; for I had an old sergeant in my parish who used to come once a quarter to have the necessary paper signed for obtaining his pension; and it was this very man who had put Napoleon in his coffin. I related to my broth( r the following story which the old sergeant had told me. He had originally been q shoemaker; and as he had conducted himself well in the ranks he was promoted to be a sergeant. On account of his calling he was able to amuse himself by shoemaking,while at the same time he could fulfil the duty assigned to him at St. Helena, which was to see Napoleon twice every day—morning and evening, and to telegraph ,that he had done so to the Governor of the Island. He went to the House at Longwood every morning, and tried to give as little annoyance as possible in the performance of his duty. Napoleon knew the object of his visit, and always endeavoured to put himself in the old sergeant's way, so that by-and-by a sort of friendship sprang up between the two. The sergeant's sentry box was built in a very prominent position, so that every ship arriving from or leaving for India could be seen, and the view of the bay was very beautiful. Napoleon was fond of coming to the sentry box and amusing himself by watching the vessels and looking at the sea. He generally introduced himself with the words, "I come to see you." But if any vessel arrived in the bay the ex-Emperor made himself scarce, for he was greatly annoyed by ,the visitors who crowded to see him. In order to escape this annoyance he hada sunken terrace six feet deep made, in which he could walk without being seen. This quiet, monotonous mode of life went on day by day. He was always cheerful, always kindly and considerate for those about him. " It used to sadden me," said the sergeant to me, "at times when he came to see me, because he tried so many little devices to get me away from my apartments for a few minutes. I had learned by experience that this was not a prudent thing on my part; for the poor Emperor used on any such oppor- tunity to unfasten the huts c,f my rabbits, saying, 'lf lam prisoner, don't see why you should be.' I had often difficulty in catching my pets again." At length Napoleon was taken ill; and his illness was a long and trying one. He was watched and treated by his own medical attendant, and nursed by his own servants. But still the old sergeant's duty led him to see the invalid twice every day, and many were the kind words passed between the shoemaker and the great General. Napoleon slowly faded away; and when he died there was not a servant about him who could do those offices for the dead which humanity demands. The old sergeant was summoned and laid him out. The undertaker was sent for from St. Helena to measure him for his coffin. Three coffins were made, two of wood and one of lead. It was then discovered that he had ordered in his will that he was to be buried in all his regimentals, and wearing his cocked baton his head and his sword. The surgeon embalmed the body; but there was nothing they could find to put the heart into except his silver mug, for which the silver- smith made a cover by melting down five franc pieces. The coffins were brought, and the body was put in. But the dimensions had been taken for the body alone ; there was not sufficient width for the cocked hat. By way of compromise the cocked hat was placed upon the breast; the sword was packed closely by the side ; and the mug containing the heart was placed between the legs. The leaden coffin was soldered up, and the burial took place three miles from Longwood, in a vault of great depth, excavated out of the solid rock.

This tale I related to my brother, who saw that it gave such details as would afford the best possible identification of the body. My brother took an early opportunity of repeat- ing the whole story to the physician who was appointed to go to St. Helena. I was sitting in my room a few days after this when a Government messenger from the War Office was announced. I wondered what he could want, and naturally fancied I his errand to be connected with some of the emigration schemes with which I was at that time much busied. He brought me a summons to attend a meeting at the War Office on an early day. I went at the time appointed, and found a number of officers and statesmen assembled. The Chairman said to me-- You are, I believe, the brother of Professor Quekett ? " I replied that I was, and he then asked me to tell the story I had related to my brother. I told them all that the old sergeant had communicated to me, and they thanked me very warmly, say- ing that I had furnished the Commissioners with the strongest proofs for identification of the body.
