div.head: By Philip Snowden, M.P.
div.p: By Philip Snowden, M.P.
IS THE CONDITION OF THE WORKERS
IMPROVING?
SOME BOARD OF TEA DR FACTS.

The annual report on labour statistics issued by the Board of Trade is a mine of useful information on the condition of the labouring classes of the United Kingdom. It is a volume which should be in the hands of all who Nrite or speak on Labour questions as it will provide them with abundant material for pointing morals and adorning

tales. It gives the 'facts, so far as they are known at the Board of Trade, relating to wages, hours of labour, prices, cost of living, state of employment, the housing of the people, the various agencies for working class improvement, and, indeed, almost everything one could desire information upon touching labour conditions is to be found in this Is. 4d. volume of three hundred pages.

the figures relate to each of the yearsl since 1901, and the sad fact which forces itself upon the mind of the person who gives a close study to these statistics is that there is no real movement upward in the industrial condition of the working classes. Their con- dition varies from year to year, wages reductions and wages increases alternate, reductions in the hours of labour alternate ' with increases, but the net result of ten years ups and downs is that labour stands certainly in no better position, but in reality is prob- ably considerably worse. In seven of the last ten years there has been a net reduction of wages, which amounted in the aggregate to more than the increases which were secured in time three years when increases were registered. If it had not been for the increases which were given in the mining industry in 1907 the tale would have been a sorry one indeed.

div.head: SOME TELLING FIGURES.
div.p: SOME TELLING FIGURES.

I Wages at the end of 1910 stand lower than they did ten years ago, the wages on coal mining being represented now by the I index figures of 89.65 compared with 100 in , 1900. In no trade has there been more I agitation these last ten years for increase of 'wages than among the railway men, but all that the ten years agitation has been able to Ido is represented by an average increase of I 334 d a week. The wages of agricultural labourers in all parts of the United Kingdom have risen since 1900, but most of all in Ireland where the increase is equal to over 8 per cent. But one very serious feature of the returns in regard to changes in the rates of wages is the fact that, notwithstanding that the last two years have been records in the matter of foreign trade, in the year 1909 the wages of the workers went down by £69,000, and last year the increase (the first for four years) was only £13,891. If labour is not able to do better than that when trade is exceptionally good it really looks as if its power to force up wages by the old methods had lost its potency. In that connection, too, another striking thing emerges, namely the fact that an increase in the volume of foreign trade does not appear to make any impression on the condition of employment. Ten years ago, when the volume of our foreign trade was little more than two-thirds what it was last year, the percentage of unemployed was 31 whereas last year it was 41, and in the previous year it was 77. These facts appear to point to the conclusion that the output per worker is greatly increasing, and that this is largely responsible for the increase in the number of unemployed and for the con- sequent difficulty to enforce better wages and better conditions.

div.head: PURCHASING POWER
div.p: THE PURCHASING POWER

Wages are earned to be spent, and there- fore their value must be considered in relationship to their purchasing power. While wages have been going down the cost of living has been going up, and at the end of 1910 the wholesale prices of 45 leading articles were 88 per cent. higher than in 1900. If we take the year 1901 the increase is just under 12 per cent. It follows there- fore that the workers are very much worse off now than they were ten years ago, and I when this fact is taken in connection with the great increase in the wealth of the country in the meantime, there is surely a strong case for something being done to get for the wage workers a fairer share of the wealth which they help to create in such abundance. The price of corn is about 19 per cent, higher, cotton about 56 per cent., bacon 66 per cent., sugar 212 per cent., eggs 24 per cent.; while there have been reductions in the price of barley and oats, potatoes, mutton, tea, coffee, and Paraffin. The aver- age price of the 41b. loaf in 1901 was 512 d., and in 1910 it was 5'79d.

The figures in regard to the sums paid by the leading trade unions for unemployment benefit show very forcefully the need for something on the lines of the Unemployed Insurance scheme. In the last two years the 100 leading trade unions have paid to their out of work members a sum of £1,949,000, nearly two million pounds. To show how hard the funds of the unions have been hit by the unemployment of the last two years it may be mentioned that these payments for unemployment are more than double the average of the annual payments for the previous eight years. Last year 35 per cent. of the total income of 100 unions mentioned was disbursed in out of work benefit. The Trade Unions have saved the rates of this country tens of millions by the sacrifices the members have made to help their fellow workmen in times of need. They have a strong claim on the State for generous con- sideration. In addition to the sums paid for unemployment benefit the trade unions spend over half a million a year on accident, sick, and funeral benefits, while 14 per cent, of their total income is devoted to the payment of superannuation to their aged members. The State has been a laggard in following up the work which these working class organ- isations, and the friendly societies,have been doing.

div.head: (')TIIER.SELF-HELP AGENCIES.
div.p: (')TIIER.SELF-HELP AGENCIES.
The friendly societies have done a magnifi- cent work, and the volume under considera- tion gives some astounding figures of the

magnitude of their operations. At the end of 1908, which is the last year for which the figures are available, there were no less than 13,777,433 members of friendly societies, including the cotlecting societies, which account for about half the total membership. These figures are vet y eloquent of the anxiety and struggles of the poor to provide for times of need. Such self-help is deserving of all the assistance which the State may be dis- posed to grant. . . . .

_ We have seen how the worker is denied an increasing share of the increase in the national wealth, how, in fact, his lot is getting harder from year to year, we have seen how hard he struggles to make some provision against adversity, but that does not exhaust the recital of the hardships of the worker's life. The statistics in regard to accidents disclose the appalling fact that there are over 4,000 workpeople killed every year in the course of their employment, and no less than 154,357 accidents were reported last year. This is a heavier toll of life than is taken in a great war, and this, it should be remembered, is not an occasional calamity, but a state of things which is constant. The Workmen's Compensation Act is a blessing to those who have the misfortune to meet with an accident. The figures show that in 1900 a sum of £2,274,238 was paid in the principal industries as compensation for accidents. It is impossible to conceive what comfort this has given to thousands of work- men's homes.

div.head: TRADE UNION PROGRESS.
div.p: TRADE UNION PROGRESS.

The figures of the membership of trade unions show a slight decline for the year 1901 i as compared with those for the previous years, but this is easily accounted for. There had been a great rush into the unions in 1906 and 1907 and some of these new recruits bad never been more than nominal members. In the last two years their names have been written off. The figures show that there is a tendency going on to amalgamate trade unions. The number of unions now is 129 fewer than in 1900, although the number of members is about 400,000 more. Fewer unions and more unionism is a motto which the unions might adopt with advantage.

There has been a remarkable increase in emigration during the past few years. Last year was not exactly a record year. It was a record for the last ten years in the number of persons leaving the country, but after deducting the number of persons who came back it fell just below the record year of 1907. The number of persons who left these shores in 1910 to countries out of Europe was 398,119. These are the flower of our popula- tion largely.

The light of love was in her eyes, the ioy• *us feeling, of youth tapping at her heart, She sang blithely, snatch... of Eastern songs, Is she tripped across the lawn and nodded pay to Niggins, who sat in his punt ledger- lag for barbel. A broad !grin of welcome 'Widened hie mouth. The late purloiner of men's goods was living, no he considered, • moral and decent life. There were two things which Niggins feared in this world; them were the criminal law, and losing the regard of Mary Smith, the buxom cook, who had subdued the animal in the man and made him human. This dishonest fence, bred in a sink of iniquity, had succumbed to the fascinations of a woman whom he had originally intended should aid him in rob- bing her master's honor. For thin reason the cracksman and receiver of the Seven Dials bad retired upon his laurels, dwelling in res- pectability, though it must be confessed it was on the proceeds of his rascality. No more portable articles would be " snick," nor gold thrown into the smelting pot; he be- lieved himself to be thoroughly secure in his Camden Town retreat, not, caring a snap either for " narks" or the police. His re- gard for the Kidder, the name befitowed by him on Blandford, was the worship of the rank and file for a clever general. Ile ex- pected • reward for his cunning, and right well he knew the generosity of him whom he served.

Angling was dull sport this morning, for the fish were off feed, and it w” with keen and eager eyes that he kept a look out for Lawson, whom he expected to see on the bank at any moment. "I love Michael, and Michael loves me," hummed Aide. ThV words were overheard by Miriam, who happend to be coming through the French windows.

"Are you not ashamed, Aide?" she said in harsh reproof. "The subject is distasteful to me, and you are in the glare of the Run. Come into thin cool room, yovir complexion will be ruined." " My complexion can take care of itself. I require an answer. You say that he robbed his benefactor, and in saving that you cast a stigma on the name of tine man I love, In hia defence I say he is not a vulgar common thief. Of what is he accused, is theft of money or of jewellery? What did be steal' Indirett charges amount to nothing mare than malicious 'dander, all the world owns that. Ile was seen leaving the Khan's cham- ber. Did you see him?" Miriam, now thoroughly in control of her- mit, wan in no way moved, and she answered "No." Then her lips cloned tightly. " Who told you?" asked Aide, her persist- enc7 increasing. "I do not betray confidence," said Miriam coldly.

no, that would be unfair." Miriam was quick witted, and seeing mis- chief brewing dashed into scolding. "That worthless servant of the Khan has infatuated you. If he was not guilty of taking that which was not big, why did he leave so ab- ruptly? Did he bid yon good-bye?" Aide \Val silent. The colour on her face deepened, and she planed nervously with the roses which she carried in her hands. "He did not, but stole away, leaving you to wear the willow.. Poor ehila." . .

The girl bit her lip. "He had good cause, or he would not have gone," she said at last. "Where is he? Skulking in some out-of. the-way corner, dreading • prosecution?" Aide remained provokingly incredulous, "Hive up this man he is unworthy of you. Have you no maidenly pride?" Aide smiled. She was blunting the edge of Ifiriam's private spleen. Are you fool enough—do you imagine he cares for you?" "I am sure he does," was the girl's confi- dent retort.
"His conduct forbids such a conclusion, Miriam exclaimed.
"Perhaps. Yet Michael is neither capri- cious nor heartless," Aide rejoined. "How little do you know the deceitfulness of men."

--"48-it jealousy which prompts you to say all this?" said the girl at • venture. "Jealousy!" Miriam echoed. She gave the daring girl a look cold, steady, and wither- ing. "I stoop too low to bandy words with you. You insult me. lam a daughter of the Khan." Angry tears started to her eyes. She could have struck the girl. "I waste affection on • man of his lowly birth? Who were his parents?" "'Yes, who were they? I believe you could Inform him, but you will not. Does Michael stand between you and money?" "I am my father's heiress," said Miriam haughtily. "True. But where is his wealth? Is it hoarded away? In what shape is it?" Miss Trafford's face underwent several changes before she replied, and her voice snook as she spoke again, br she was furious at this catechism.
"Michael Lawson is • penniless beggar, • ereature a my father's; but he cares no more for you than I do for him." "He is my chosen husband," said the girl steadily. "tour husband!"
"WET; witTii;;;3 hueband. The men I love and you would take from me. But that you cannot do." Aide was no longer a timid girl. Lose had transformed her into • courageous Woman.

Mariam calmed her rising anger, recognis- ing that Aide was getting out of hand; and. not wishing the dispute to lead to an open rupture, she remained silent for some little time. Then in subdued tones, aceompanicd by a cutting sneer, she said, "My dear child you will be wise to be guided by your elders. In .your innocence you imagine that Lawson is an love with you. Were you needy, would hit devotion endure the teat/ No It is your fortune that be covets, not you, my dear child."
"My fortune !" echoed Aide, astounded. "What else do you suppose is his induce- ment. Yourself Bub !"

"You hare told me that I am living on your bounty, and have always warned me not to set your authority at defiance. Now you talk as though I was posnesw'd of means. Am I rich, mid are you only pretending charity, an almoner of doles for conscience Fake? My for- tune! Where is it? Am I rich?"

"I have done my duty, lavishing on you all I could. Fortnne you have none." Miriam, angered at her slip of the tongtt., made for the door. But Aide was not no sully satisfied. tier interest was thoroughly aroused, and she pressed for an answer. "Am I also an heiress? Have I property of sey own?' Miriam sauntered pant the persistent girl and gazed from the easement at'Niggins fish- ing in his punt, little dreaming of the influ- ence that in daym to come he would exercise over her schemes.

property .1(1. You shall have an adequate income for your station, provided that you marry the man I select." Miriam opened the windows wide, and was stepping out into the garden, but Aide held her by the gown. "My husband must be my choice; not yours. I am not your bond slave, and in that matter I intend to please myself." "Wilful and ungrateful. Don't clutch my avail, please. you are creasing it, .1110 Miriam coldly. Smoothing her Mirt and ar- ranging the crumpled, clinging material into graceful folds, she seated herself in an arm. chair. mying, "Let on bring our unpleasant morning's talk to an end. :..4o far our dispute has not been edifying." She opened a copy of the "Telegraph," trying to find the ad- vertisements in the agony column. Rodripies having proposed this method of communica- tion. Aide sorted some skeins of coloured silk and began embroidering a slipper in gold thread. She stitched and stitched, leer thoughts keeping pace with her nimble fin- gers. At last the work dropped into her lap and she stared idly at the scudding clouds. Her naturally cheerful tempera- ment was saddened. She was good and pure herself, and her instinct was to think of ell men and women as the name. That morntiq she had received a rude shock. Simple ants unworldly vs she was, she had sense enough to comprehend that the late Khan had de- frauded her, and that Mirinm was a partner in the deception. She was fully assured there had been a gross miscarriage of justice. It was clear to her that she was entitled to money. But left to her by whom? A strange darkness fell upon her mind. Of her parents she knew no more than did her lover. When ever she had questioned her guardian, the Khan had invariably replied: "When you are of age, your parents wishes must be carried out." A CHILD', D.Tfl.—An Inquiry wan held by Mr. T. Ridgway, coroner, at Hatton on Monday evening relating to the death, which took place on Sunday, of Albert Sutter, aged 2 years and 9 months, lon of Jsmes Rutter, gardener, of Hatton. Edith Rutter, mother of deceased, said that on Friday she heard her son crying and founds piece of wire in his throat. The wire was on the broken end of a whip stock. After extracting It his throat bled a little and she gave the child some water and it afterwards played about in the garden. At 4 p.m. on Sunday she noticed tie child breathing heavily and sent for the doctor, but death took place on Sunday at 6.15 p.m. Dr. Bower said he went to the house and found the boy in a state of collapse. lie wile Informed by Mrs. Rutter what had happened. His opinion was death due to pneumonia accelerated by the accident. A verdict in accordance with Dr. Bowers evidence was returned.

SCHOOLMASTER FINED FOR ASSAULT.—A case of more than natal interest was dealt with at I.ymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday by Mr. A. Watkin (in the chili') Major J. E. G. Groves and Mr. S. W. Oonld, when Mr. John James Borrowes,beadmaster of Warburton School, was summoned for assaulting William Chorlton and Oliver Wareham, two echoolboys residing at Warburton—William Chorlton, aged 12, said that he now attended Seaman. School, Altrincham, but up to 17 months ago he attended defen- dants school. On the afternoon of the 13th ult., his school was closed so he and Wareham went into the village to a shop near the 'school, to buy some sweets. They got there about 2.30 and when the boys came out I at 2.40 for play time they spoke to them. When the I I play time vas finished Mr. Borrow. told them to go away. Thereupon, they went down the road for a hundred yards and watched a farmer load a cart. About ten minutes afterwards Mr.Borrowee came out of tbe schoolgarden, ran after them and when he caught them up 'Mont 800 yards awn,' he hit wanesn on the ears, and struck him in the ribs knocking him down. He also hit Wareham on the face.—ln reply to Mr. Richard Cobbett, solicitor of Mancheeter, who repre- sented the defendant, witness denied that he and his companion arrived at the school at 2 o'clook and also that they did not go away when Mr. Borrowes asked them. He ass hurt very much by the blow which defendant gave him.— Oliver Wareham, aged 12, corro- borated Chorlton'e evidence.—Harry Ball, aged 13, and , a scholar at the school of the defendant arid that he now Mr. Borrower go up to the boysand in consequence of what lie said to them they went away end be did not see them return.—Mr. Cobbett eddressing the magistrates raid the case was a very trumpery one and very incomprelmesible because the suggestion on the part of the boys was that they went away immediately after Mr. Borrowes had asked them to and that he only went to them ten minutes af terwarda— In his evidence the defendant (who was corroborated by two schoolboys) said that he twice caked the boys to go because their presence was dis- tracting the pupils' attention. They went away, but returned, to he again requested them to leave. They did no, but when they got eeverel yards away, they ' mounted the railing and waved their hands to him. lie , then went after them and hit them, but only slightly. Indeed, they did not cry. The magistrates retired and on returning the Chairman said that they were quite sure that the complainant. went to annoy the school-1 master and upset his work, but at the same time they were advised that a technical tumult had been com- mitted and they would have to inflict e nominal fine of Is. in each case including costs.

WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. The anniversary sermons in connection with this place were pr ached on Sunday last by the Rev. E. B. Keeling. In the morning Mr. Keeling took his text From xvi. Romans 5 verse. He emphasized the necessity of religion being part of our lives and said it would he good for people to reelize that the three hours spent in church on Sundays was the smallest pert of their religion. A church is not stone, bricks end wood, it is people and where there are no people there in no church. There is no mention in the Bible of. Christian place of worship, and for the first 100 years that Christianity wae in the world, there was no place to worship in. How did they manege it Eve'', house was a church where prays meeting were regularly held. theca • home in Warrington to.dety where if digester came to the church they wonld open their doors end ray toter go in and pray there? A church of the living God in every house. Is this possible ! In coradusion he said he would like the church to never be happy anima they were ever in the atmosphere of theliving God and be urged all present never to rest satisfied until they got a church in every bone. In the afteraoun a flower service was held presided over by Mr. 11. Tarlatan of Pedgate. A very interesting and instructive addregs was given to the scholars and teacher. by Mrs. Gladding.

She showed how the wind was na(ure's great sanitary inspector, always bringing sweetness in its train, and gave many Must, Janos to prove that it was the great husbandman and y nysician. She said she liked to think . .

of the wind ass revealer of beauty, end showed bow God's epirit could be compared to the wind. In the evening the Rev. E. B. Keeling preached frnm St. John, ii. 14v. He said that religion demands the best that man and woman can put into it. Christianity in the days of John was not an easy thing? it was very difficult. If we look at the characteristics of the men of whom John spoke, we find their strength inspired and victorious. Strength is the strongest word in any language, and the strength that will endure in poverty, lonelinme, and in the hour of death is the strength which Jesus Christ can give. The measure of a men's inspiration is how much of the love of God he has in hie been. Love is expensive and causes pain. The only way to deal with the evil one is to torn him out. The temptations of the olden days are very much like the temptations of to-day. We knee to conquer, and there is no victory in always keeping away from peril,so the very glories of the Christian life are in its peril. Splendour of character and splendour of heroism are only practicable in Jesus Christ, He urged all to work no that eventually they would go to that place where the •iotors crowns are given and where there is peace for evermore. div.head: CONFERENCE OF GUILDS OF HELP.
div.p: CONFERENCE OF GUILDS OF HELP.

The fourth annual Conference of Guilds of Help wee held 0 Tueadny, Wednesday, and Thureday of this week, in Birmingham, where about 3JO representatives of flfty Guilds foregathered fort frank and free die- mission on various aspects of Uuild work. Warrington lane represented by Mr. W. J. Rowland (secretary) as I delegate, end by Mr. end Mir. J. A. Raneorne, Menne. IF. W. Madeley, and Jame. Rill, as visitors:. . _ . .

The Conference commenced by a well attended public meeting at the Midland Institute, the speaker. being Mr. Strel-fileitlaorl, M.P., and Dr. Devil, the bead muter of Rugby. Dr. David delivered a Iloe address, based on his Bristol experiences, and inspired through. out by a high ideal of the guilds' pounibilities and opportunities for noble service. Wednesdsy was a very full day. At 10 o'clock delegates and visitors assembled at Queen'. Gallego, , Paradise-street, to hear and discuss rapers on The Relations of Guilds of Help with public authorities such as "The Poor Law," " Public Health and Educstiont" " Police." The papers proved to be sound and practical, and were followed by helpful short speeches of five minutes each. hir. W. J. Rowland con- tributed his quota to the seismal discussion. From 12 noon an hour was devoted to impromptu questions and answers, on many matters pertinent to Guild Work. Perhaps some of the questions and answers were notes impromptu as apt eared but they bore on important points, and so a proatlble hour was spent. After the luncheon interval the delegates and visitors again assembled, this time in the Council Chamber under the Chairmanship of tub Rt. Hon. the Lordjfileyor of Birmingham to hear a paper read on one of the most importsnt and pressing needs of Guild effort, •ix Mutuel Registration of Assistance." A record of all applications received and assistance reodered by every charitable and religious organization in a district is absolutely necessary if helpful agencies are to he co-ordinated. Ways and meson of obtaining this common record, and the difficulties in the way, caused a free discussion and numerous short speeches, mostly to the point. It was interesting to learn that in Liverpool the Boards if Guardians had contributed .CBOO to cover cost of registration in that district, and that definite progress had been made there for obtain. log the assistance of relief of all organizations. A ;dement interlnde followed. The Lord Mayor end Lady !Mayoress generously entertained the delegates and friends to tea in a handsome hall in the Council House. The hospitality can greatly appreciated. In the evening the papers were read on "The helper " •nd "The district head "by two well- known Guild workers. Thursday Wes delegatee busines. day. The conference was quite a success and shows once more that the Guilds of Help have splendid material in their ranks and that by tact, enthusiasm, sympathy and knowledge, a band of zealous voluntary workers is growing hp Tr reared and equipped to wage continuous war against the complex problems of poverty and distress.

A sad accident occurred on Tuewlay at kfarah Lock, on the blanche/der Ship Canal, near Runcorn. A Salt Union steamer was towing. barge up the canal when it groundbd. The mate of the barge, Harry Barnett, aged , twenty-six, of Wilmington Park, went to release the towing rope. A terrific thunderstorm swept over Newton and Earleatown between sin and seven on Saturday even- ing. A thatched cottage in the neighbourhood of the Newton Farm School was struck by the lightning,and was net on fire. div.head: BLACKSMITH'S SAD END,
div.p: BLACKSMITH'S SAD END,

An inquest wee held at the Warrington Police Station on Monday by Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, on the body of William Hall, aged 68, a blacksmith's striker of Newt° n-le.Willoss, who died at the War- rington Infirmary on the 12th isn't. having been admitted to that instituti,n on the 2cd inst. suffering from crushed toes. Deceased was working at the Vulcan Foundry, Herlestown on the 2nd inst. and while helping with a crane to put a coupling rod into the furnace, the chain on the pulley plug came out of the socket and the rod fell on the floor catching his toes. Mr. Amos, solicitor, speared for the Company, Mr. White for the relativesousd Ste. Pollard 11. M. Inspector of Factories was also present. Mary Hall, widow of the deceased, said that on the morning of the 20d inst.' he left to go to work about 6.30 and in the evening she heard that he had met with en accident and had been taken to the Warrington Infirmary. On the 4th inst., she went to the Institution and new her husband who told her that he had been helping to place the coupling rod into the furnace and ihe chain of the putty broke and the rod fell on his foot. She received& telegram on the 12th Inst, stating that he had died. . . _

Henry Williamson a blacksmith, 5, London-road, Vulcan, said that about 4.30 on the 2nd net,i he wan engaged in putting a 6 cwt. coupling rod into the furnace. The deceased was holding the rod in place so that it would go in the furnace, when it fell to the floor. He did not actually witness the accident but saw the deceased jumping about. , . '`

Dr. Tineley, junior house surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, said that the great toe and the second toe of the left foot were crushed. On May 4th the amputation of the croaked toed was performed. Blood poisoning developed and the man died about 12.5 on the 11th of May. In his opinion death was due to blood poisoning , following upon the injury to the toes.—The jury returned • verdict of Accidental &iota," and the Coroner remarked that the Factory Inspector could find no fault with the machinery, the same having been going for • number of years.

- Sir,—Will you please allow me to correct a slight error in your otherwise excellent and interesting report appearing in to-day'e issue of the" Examiner " of the annual Council meetings of the Women' s Liberal Federalion, held during the present week at Manchester. Von state that For the first time in the hist,ry of the Federation these meetings have been held out of the Metropolis." It Ns.uu my privilege, with Mrs. Clay, to represent the Warring- ton Branch of the Federation at the Council meetings held at Halifax in May 1911:1, that being the outcome of a suggestion at the London meeting of 1902 (when! was also present), of the advisability of holding the Councils alternately in London and one of the I'rovincial cities or towns. The suggestion Wag then received with almost unanimous approval hut for some reasons with which I am unacquainted the idea him not been quite accurate'y carried out. Believe me yours very truly, (Mrs) R. A. O'BRIEN. 125, Wilderspool Causeway, Saturday, May Pth, 1911.

div.head: Council and the Suffrage.,
div.p: The Council and the Suffrage.,

Sir,— I em sure your readers do not desire to follow a prolonged controversy between Miss Waring and myself on this subject and anticipating in the near future an editorial note to that effect I now submit my final contribution. thiginally I wrote to yon, Sir, protesting that the Council Chamber should be utilitsel for suffrage propaganda and I am quite satisfied to have Miss Waring's own words confirming the fact that the matter dealt with was quite outside ordinary business. I agree that it wan extraordinary business. his Waring's letter includes a good deal of matter having reference to the Anti-Suffrage canvas and vainly endeavours to discredit the same. If she has no better implements than those which are utilised her efforts result in an inglorious failure. In the lace of a postcard canvas in N.W. Manchester the only answer I receive is a quotation from Sir George Kemp's speech " I have reason to believe that they are entirely with me." Will Mi-s Waring kindly peruse page til of the Anti-Suffrage Review whereon she will find a list of districts where results were obtained by poAteard aud produce prod t r discredit any one of them. Take one, does she say that the canvas in N.W. Manchester is incorrect ? Amongst the " microscopic portion " of her sex of whom Miss Waling has "long been ashamed '' it would be interesting to learn if she includes Her late Majesty Queen Victoria. As to a debate at Warrington next September or Ocmber.there is plenty of time and if Miss Waring desires my address the Editor is authorised to furnish it. But will interest not have evaporated then having regard to what the "'limes" save as to the decision of ,the House of Commons on the Women's Enfran- chisement Bill, namely, that it " will be generally interpreted as tantamount ton sentence of extinction and the " Daily Mail " adds that " unless the Govern- ment find time for it, it will dier."? - Yours &c., JOHN W. O. BEAUMONT. Manchester, May 10th,

Mr. New and a Battersea Argument. Sir, —While passing the meeting held by the Progres- sive Labour League last Monday evening toy attention was caught by an argument Mr. New was advancing iu support of Free Trade as against tariff Reform the substance of which was as follows A certain flint in Battersea bad been eaabled by the introduction of new machinery, to produce a certain class of goods at a very much quicker rule than formerly ; also with the aid of this improved machinery, one man can now do the work of six men,consequently the displaced men were dismissed, the individual respousiblejor their dismiesal being a Tory M.P. The fact that he was a ry M.Pand Tariff Reformer was especially emplia- siaed. Now, Sir, I think this is playing the game rather low down. Certainly, Hr. New did tint any that had the employer been a Free Trader the men would not have been dismissed, Ind that was the impre.ion he wished to leave with his hearers, at least no it seemed to me. Pere sally, I hold no brief for either Tariff Reform or the Tory Party, both are diametrically opposed to the true interesta of the workers, will I fail to see where the lan !ed bless- ings of Free Trade come in. Under Free Trade the rich are getting richer, and the poor are becoming relatively poorer. Mr. New must know that Liberal capitalists and employers of Labour are eapible of dealing— as they often do deal quite as ruthlessly with their work people aa are Tory capitalist.. The fault rents not with the capitaliso, but with the son- tern, the standard of morality is always set by the things beneath us. Free Trade may be better than Protection under the present system, but neither Free Trade nor l'rotection will solve the p .verty or unemployment problem. Both Liberal and Tr,ry employers have stood t-gether to resist the j.t demands of Labour. Labours emancipat:on will come, not through the Liberal or Tory party, but through its own united effort.—Youra truly, JAS. HAMPSON. 80, Ohlham-street Warrington. May Ilith. 1311.

div.head: Mr. Crosfieid and National Service
div.p: Mr. Crosfieid and National Service

Sir, - Mr. Arthur Crostield, in his speech at Bridge Foot, as reported in last Saturday's papers, apparehtly tried to throw dust in the eyes of his audience by suggesting that the supporters of National Service are ipso f0..t0 supporters of taxing the people's korl. This is a regrettable suggestion, for it disregards certain truths well-knoon to the politicians of Warrington. Surely, Mr. Crosfield must have been so moved by his own eloquence that he forgot that Mr. It. Roberts, J P., whose name is renowned throughout South Lanca- shire as a sound and eloquent Liberal, is the chairman of the Executive Committee of the local division of the National Service [Pogue, while under him, on that committee, sit at least four other champions of Free Trade. The late member has always been regarded by friend and foe with respect as a member, but in linking National Service to Pro- tection, he hits many staunch Liberal, and old members of the league. ins distinctly unjustifiable manner. Mr. Arthur Crosfield msy defend himself by saying that he referred in his remarks to the movement usa whole throughout Great Britain. But here again ova man who has been on iutiinate U rals with the leaders of the National Service League, he must know the truth. J. S. Mill and Adam Smith have often been quoted by Mr Crosfield and his supporters, yet twice in 1870 J. S. Mill wrote letter& which today would be attributed to Lord Roberts, while Adam Smith bad PO doubt that manhood service was the only Kure principle. One of the earli,st promoters of the league was the Presbyte, inn Elder, the late Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P. for Flintshire, who won a determined and consistent Liberal to the day of his death. A colleague of Mr. Crosfield's, in the House, Colonel Seely, the present fader-Secretary of State for War, was one of the three original M.P.'s, mem- bers of the N.S.L. in the 1000 Parliament. It was only a few days ago that Colonel Seely spoke of com- pulsion to the Veteran Reserve and was immediately greet-d with cheers. MrArthrir Crosfield must know that Tariff Reform has nothing whatever to do with National Service. Why. then, mislead the public ? llama(' of tusking unvrarrarded suggestions con- necting Protection with compulsory military training, the true Liberal attitude would be
Can the League jus•ify itself on general principles of reason and commonsense?"

Such speeches as that made wilfully by Mr, Crosfield only entangle present polit'cadpassion lot, vital national issue. He is, in fact, driving a question affecting the community of interests and of ideals which ought to be the inheritance cf every citizen,into the obscurity of partisan prejudice, much against the wishes of many of his former suppurters, life-long Liberals and Free Traders, who believe,with thorough conviction, that the National Service League has logic. fac.ta and patriotism on its tide. . . . . . .

div.head: Damage by Lightning at Warrington.
div.p: Damage by Lightning at Warrington.

Wirrington was visited by one of the most violent thunderstorms of rev at yea -s at abmt half-past five on Saturday eveni:.g. Following a perfect summer afternoon, there were heavy peals of thunder, a territir downpour of rain and bail, and unusually vivid lightning. In all parts of the tosn d image, was done to property, aid the low.lyi.,g stre,ts were flooded, the inhabitants stilTerl g great inconvenience through the inrush of water to their cellars, and even t , the living rooms. Many chimney pots and gable ends were struck by lightning, and at the Stag Hoe!. Lower Walton, the electric wires fused, but fortunately the flames were extinguished before any serious mischief was done. Two yonng ladies, Mies Lily Bowers. of Walton-road, and Miss Nelly Hughes if Ellesinere-road, St aikton Heath, while sheltering from the storm in the porch at the Stag 11,tel were struck by liglyning. They were dared for sonic time. but att,r restoratives had been applied they were able t , walk home. A youth who was doing some work in the cellar at his hune in Manchester-road was struck on the hand and was for a short time incapacitated. The lightning playing upon the overhead electric wires in Bridge-street provided a remarkable spectacle, a sheet of flame running the whole length of the street. The tram service was interrupted for sonue hours. The ears were " held up " through the lightning severing the cables of tits ground boxes in Winmarleigh-street and Manchester-road. No time was lost, however, in rectifying the damage. In 40 minutes the Stockton Heath and Latchford services were re-opened, but it was not until ten minutes past eight that the service on the Sankey route was resumed
